messages.body_plain:
That was indeed very useful.

Sadly, I can't snap my fingers and download the package to the work computers, but I can
play on my home computer... On my (Windows-based) R, when I switch the locale to Hebrew,
I can type Hebrew but the device coughs when it tries to interpret or plot it (warnings, etc.).
And the standard pdf output is replaced by dots, and more warnings.

However, when I used CairoPDF, the Hebrew letters were in fact rendered correctly, though
left-to-right. Assuming this works on the work computers (which are also Windows-based),
then I'm halfway to a solution, which is progress.

So, thank you again!

And now to find a way to reverse the text order, which might end up being a "macro"
of sorts.

Ari

On Wednesday, February 29, 2012 3:07:53 PM UTC-8, Jonathan Rosenblatt wrote:

> This is undoutably a character encoding issue.
> Bottom line- I was unable to solve the problem. Here is what I learned on the way...

>
> Since version 2.10, R uses UTF-8 for internal representation of characters. This is why you should be able to see hebrew on screen and in "standard" plots (say, using the windows device on MS Windows). It will also work in RStudio (I didn't check which graphic device it uses) but not on a Mac using X11 (no text) nor Quartz (inverted hebrew text). Linux will use only X11 so I am not optimistic regarding hebrew plots.
> Sadly pdf and postscript devices supported only single-byte encodings, which UTF is not one of them. There are several Hebrew single-bute encodings (say ISO 8859-8 <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO/IEC_8859-8>). Sadly, I was unable to call them since the encodings available to pdf() and postscript() are the ones with .enc files in the grdevices library. There is no appropriate .enc file for any of the single-byte hebrew encodings.
>
> All was not lost once I found this:
> http://www.stat.auckland.ac.nz/~paul/R/PDF/pdfEncoding.html <http://www.stat.auckland.ac.nz/%7Epaul/R/PDF/pdfEncoding.html>
> Sadly, the simple solution did not work on my Mac (with native cairo) and I didn't try the hard solution. I also tried the Cairo package with the CairoPDF function, without any luck. There is however the hope that it might work on a Linux machine with native Cairo support.
>
> I hope this helped.
>
> J

> Modern scientific and engineering research relies heavily on computer programs, which analyze experimental data and run simulations. In fact, you would be hard-pressed to find a scientific paper (outside of pure theory) that didn’t involve code in some way. Unfortunately, most code written for research remains closed, even if the code itself is the subject of a published scientific paper. According to an editorial in Nature, this hinders reproducibility, a fundamental principle of the scientific method.
